meta.title: Who really said "A future startup with no patents of its own will be forced to pay whatever price the giants choose to impose"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Quoted for years as Bill Gates admitting the patent system is rigged. Wikiquote credits the line to the League for Programming Freedom, not to Gates.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A future startup with no patents of its own will be forced to pay whatever price the giants choose to impose'?
meta.ogDescription: Not from Gates’s 1991 memo. Wikiquote traces the sentence to the League for Programming Freedom’s 1991 paper against software patents.

answer.label: Not Bill Gates — the League for Programming Freedom
answer.sourceLine: The sentence circulates as a line from Gates’s internal Microsoft memo “Challenges and Strategy” (16 May 1991), by way of Fred Warshofsky’s 1994 book The Patent Wars. Wikiquote records that as a misreading of Warshofsky’s text ↗ and attributes the wording instead to the League for Programming Freedom’s 1991 paper Against Software Patents.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Bill Gates, “Challenges and Strategy” memo, 16 May 1991
A misreading of Fred Warshofsky, The Patent Wars (1994)

source.excerpt: A future startup with no patents of its own will be forced to pay whatever price the giants choose to impose. That price might be high. Established companies have an interest in excluding future competitors.
trail: Wikiquote’s Bill Gates page ↗ lists the sentence under Misattributed, records that it is cited to the “Challenges and Strategy” memo of 16 May 1991 via Fred Warshofsky’s 1994 The Patent Wars, and states that this is a misreading of Warshofsky’s text.

The same entry names the actual source as the League for Programming Freedom ↗ (1991), “Against Software Patents”, and points to Lawrence Lessig’s The Future of Ideas (2001) as an example of the misattribution appearing in print.

We could not read the League’s paper ourselves — the MIT server hosting it is unreachable from our network — so the identification here rests on Wikiquote, not on our own inspection of the 1991 document.
source.excerptNote: This is the passage in the form Wikiquote records under Misattributed ↗. We were not able to retrieve the League for Programming Freedom’s 1991 paper directly, so we have not checked the wording against the document itself.
source.rightsNote: Wikiquote identifies the wording as the League for Programming Freedom’s, first published in 1991, which is well inside US copyright — so it is treated as in copyright here. The Gates memo it is usually credited to would likewise be in copyright.

author.name: League for Programming Freedom
author.heading: About League for Programming Freedom
author.metaLine: Founded 1989 · Software-patent and interface-copyright reform group
author.bio: The League for Programming Freedom was founded in 1989 by Richard Stallman to oppose software patents and the extension of the scope of copyright, uniting developers of free and proprietary software alike. Its campaigns included the “Burn all GIFs” protest against Unisys’s enforcement of the LZW compression patent, and it published a newsletter, Programming Freedom, in eleven issues between 1991 and 1995.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The line is a favourite exhibit in software-patent arguments — an industry titan apparently conceding that the system is built to crush newcomers. The titan did not write it.

items.why: Wikiquote lists the sentence under Misattributed ↗ and states that the quotation is actually the League for Programming Freedom’s, not Gates’s.
The attribution traces back through Warshofsky’s 1994 book, but Wikiquote calls it a misreading of his text ↗ rather than a claim Warshofsky made himself.

items.who: Lawrence Lessig, The Future of Ideas (2001)
items.why: Wikiquote cites Lessig’s book ↗ as an example of the misattribution in circulation.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence belongs to the League for Programming Freedom’s 1991 paper against software patents — as Wikiquote’s Bill Gates entry sets out ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The quotation does real work in public argument: it is produced whenever someone wants to show that even the biggest software company understood patents as a toll-gate rather than an incentive. Coming from Gates, it reads as a confession.

Coming from the League for Programming Freedom — a campaigning group founded in 1989 expressly to fight software patents — it reads as what it is: an argument by people who already held that position. That is a different kind of evidence, which is why the mix-up matters.
detailsBody: Wikiquote’s note is precise about the mechanism. The sentence is cited to Gates’s “Challenges and Strategy” memo of 16 May 1991 through Fred Warshofsky’s 1994 book The Patent Wars, and it is that citation, not the memo, that went wrong: Wikiquote describes it as a misreading of Warshofsky’s text.
Once made, the error was durable enough to reach serious scholarship — Wikiquote points to Lawrence Lessig’s The Future of Ideas (2001) as an instance of the line appearing under Gates’s name.
context.pull: An argument from a campaign group is not a confession from a monopolist.
